tips.title: A pie is 360 shared out
tips.body: Picture cutting a cake for the whole class: **360° shared equally among everyone surveyed**. With 60 people, each person gets $360 \div 60 = 6°$, so a group of 21 gets $21 \times 6 = 126°$. Find the slice for **one person** first, then multiply.

tips.title: Words, whole numbers, or time?
tips.body: Ask what the data is. **Words** (colours, ways to travel): bar chart, pie chart or pictogram. **Whole numbers** (people in a car, goals): vertical line chart. **Measurements over time** (sales each month): a table and a line graph, with time along the bottom.

tips.title: Angles make 360, frequencies make the total
tips.body: Before drawing a pie chart, add your angles: they must come to **360°**. Before trusting a two-way table, check that **every row and every column** adds to its total. A total that fails is a slip you can find now rather than lose marks for later.

tips.title: Zero or zoomed?
tips.body: Read the **axis** before the bars or the line. A **bar chart** starts at **zero**, because bar heights are compared as sizes. A line graph of values far from zero, such as temperatures, is often **zoomed**, and that is fine with the break shown. It misleads when the break is hidden or the picture overstates the change: 96% to 99% filling the whole graph.

tips.title: Pictograms: whole symbols, then the part
tips.body: Count the **whole** symbols and multiply by the key, then add the **part** symbol as a fraction of the key. Key 4, three and a half symbols: $3 \times 4 + 2 = 14$. Choosing a key that divides easily into quarters or halves makes the part symbols easy to draw too.

why.matters:
A table of numbers holds the facts, but people rarely read tables. A chart turns the same facts into a picture that can be taken in at a glance, which is why charts are so common in news reports, company reports and science papers. Each kind of chart is built for one kind of question: a bar chart for *which is biggest*, a pie chart for *what share*, a line graph for *how has it changed*.

The same power makes charts easy to abuse. A picture is believed before it is checked, and a zoomed axis or an oversized symbol can make a small change look dramatic without a single false number. Knowing how each chart is built is what lets you read one critically, and draw one honestly.

examples.title: The graph that soars by three percentage points
examples.body:
A company's leaflet shows customer satisfaction over five years: 96%, 97%, 97%, 98%, 99%. On its graph the line climbs almost from bottom to top.

The trick is the vertical axis. It starts at **95%**, and nothing on the graph marks the break. On that axis the first point is 1 unit up and the last is 4 units up, so the line looks as if satisfaction has **quadrupled**. In fact it rose by **3 percentage points**, from an already high 96%.

No number on the graph is false. Only the picture is, and the picture is what most people remember. A zoomed axis is not wrong in itself, but checking where the axis starts, and whether the break is marked, is a good first habit with any chart.

visual.alt: A line graph of customer satisfaction over five years with the vertical axis starting at 95 percent, so a rise from 96 to 99 percent climbs almost the full height of the graph

examples.title: Where the money goes
examples.body:
One household spends £2400 a month. Rent is £960, food £480, transport £240, bills £360 and everything else £360.

A pie chart shows each part as a share of the whole. Every £1 gets $360 \div 2400 = 0.15°$, so rent's sector is $960 \times 0.15 = 144°$: **two fifths** of the circle, which is two fifths of the money.

That is the question a pie chart answers best: *what share?* It says at a glance that rent alone takes more than food and transport put together (£720). It would be a poor way to show how spending changed month by month, which needs a line graph.

visual.alt: A pie chart of one household’s monthly spending of £2400: rent 144 degrees, food 72, transport 36, bills 54 and other 54

examples.title: The winter peak in the electricity bill
examples.body:
A household records its electricity use each quarter for two years, in kilowatt-hours: 1300, 800, 600, 1100 in the first year and 1250, 760, 580, 1050 in the second.

Plotted as a **time series**, two patterns appear at once. Each year rises to a peak in **quarter 1**, the winter months, and falls to its lowest in quarter 3: that repeating shape is **seasonal**. And every quarter of year 2 is a little lower than the same quarter of year 1: that is the **trend**, downwards.

The trap is comparing the wrong quarters. From quarter 3 to quarter 4 of year 2, use rose from 580 to 1050, and that is winter arriving, not a sign that anything has gone wrong. Like is compared with like: the same quarter in different years.

visual.alt: A time-series line graph of a household’s electricity use over eight quarters: high in quarter 1 of each year and lowest in quarter 3, with every year-2 point a little lower than the same quarter of year 1

steps.title: Kinds of data, and the frequency table
steps.body:
Every chart starts with the question: **what kind of data is this?**

- **Categorical data** is words or labels: ways to travel, favourite colours. There is no number to add up, only a count of how many are in each category.
- **Discrete numerical data** is whole numbers that are counted: the number of people in a car, goals in a match. Nothing lies in between 2 and 3 people.
- **Time series data** is one measurement taken again and again over time: sales each month, the temperature each day.

**A frequency table** is where most charts begin. Each category or value gets one row, and its **frequency** is how many times it occurs. Data is often counted with a **tally**: a stroke for each item, with every fifth stroke drawn across the four before it, so the strokes can be counted in fives.

60 students were asked how they travel to school. The frequencies add up to **60**, the number of students asked. That total is the first thing to check in any frequency table.

visuals.alt: A frequency table of how 60 students travel to school: walk 21, bus 18, car 12 and cycle 9
A table matching data to charts: categories take a bar chart, pie chart or pictogram; whole-number data takes a vertical line chart; data over time takes a table and a line graph

check.prompt: A survey records how many pets each student owns: 0, 1, 2, 3 and so on. Which chart suits this data best?
check.solution: The number of pets is **discrete numerical data**, whole numbers with nothing in between, so **a vertical line chart** suits it: one thin line for each value. A line graph is for data over time.

markScheme.description: a vertical line chart

options: A pie chart of all the pets
A vertical line chart
A time-series line graph
A pictogram of animals

steps.title: Bar charts and dual bar charts
steps.body:
A **bar chart** shows categorical data as bars whose **heights are the frequencies**.

The rules that make one correct:

- **Frequency** goes up the vertical axis, on an even scale that **starts at 0**.
- Every bar has the **same width**, and there are **gaps** between the bars, because the categories are separate things.
- Both axes are **labelled**, and the chart has a title.

**A dual bar chart** puts two sets side by side: for each way to school, a bar for the boys and a bar for the girls, with a **key** to say which is which. It is built for *comparing* the two groups category by category. Here more boys than girls walk (12 against 9), and more girls than boys take the bus (10 against 8).

A **composite bar chart** does the same job with one bar per category, split into parts: the boys' section stacked on the girls'. The whole bar is the total, so it is read by subtracting: a bar from 0 to 21 with a split at 12 means 12 boys and $21 - 12 = 9$ girls.

visuals.alt: A bar chart of how 60 students travel to school, with equal-width bars and gaps between them: walk 21, bus 18, car 12 and cycle 9
A dual bar chart of how boys and girls travel to school, the two bars for each way side by side: walk 12 boys and 9 girls, bus 8 and 10, car 5 and 7, cycle 5 and 4

check.prompt: In a dual bar chart of how students travel to school, the boys’ bar for Bus reaches 8 and the girls’ bar for Bus reaches 10. How many students travel by bus altogether?
check.solution: Add the two bars for Bus: $8 + 10 = 18$ students.

steps.title: Pictograms and vertical line charts
steps.body:
**A pictogram** uses a symbol for a fixed number of items, given in a **key**. Here one square stands for 4 books, so:

- a whole square is 4 books;
- half a square is 2 books;
- a quarter of a square is 1 book.

To read a row, count the whole symbols, multiply by the key, then add the part. Wednesday has 4 whole symbols and a half of a symbol: $4 \times 4 + 2 = 18$ books. Every symbol must be the **same size**, or the picture lies.

**A vertical line chart** is for **discrete numerical data**: whole numbers such as the number of people in a car. It looks like a bar chart with the bars squeezed to thin lines. The thin line is the point: the values are separate whole numbers, and nothing happens between 2 people and 3 people, so a wide bar would suggest values that cannot exist.

In 30 cars passing a school, the most common number of people was 1 (14 cars), and 7 cars had 3 or more people.

visuals.alt: A pictogram of library books borrowed each weekday, one square standing for 4 books: Monday two and a half squares, Tuesday three and a half, Wednesday four and a half, Thursday one and three quarters, Friday three and a quarter
A vertical line chart of the number of people in each of 30 cars: 1 person 14 cars, 2 people 9 cars, 3 people 4 cars and 4 people 3 cars, drawn as thin lines rather than bars

check.prompt: In a pictogram, one square stands for 4 books. Friday’s row shows 3 whole symbols and a quarter of a symbol. How many books were borrowed on Friday?
check.solution: Three whole squares are $3 \times 4 = 12$ books. A quarter of a square is a quarter of 4, which is 1 book. Total: $12 + 1 = 13$ books.

steps.title: Pie charts: drawing one and reading one
steps.body:
A pie chart shows how a **whole** is shared into parts. The full circle, 360°, stands for everyone surveyed, and each category gets a sector in proportion to its frequency:

$$\text{angle} = \dfrac{\text{frequency}}{\text{total}} \times 360°$$

The neatest way is to find the angle for **one** item first. Then every sector is a single multiplication, and the angles must add up to 360°.

Reading a pie chart runs the same calculation backwards: $\text{frequency} = \dfrac{\text{angle}}{360°} \times \text{total}$.

visuals.problem: Draw a pie chart for how 60 students travel to school: Walk 21, Bus 18, Car 12, Cycle 9.

steps.note: The whole circle is shared among all 60 students.

steps.text: Multiply each frequency by 6: Walk $21 \times 6 = 126°$, Bus $18 \times 6 = 108°$, Car $12 \times 6 = 72°$, Cycle $9 \times 6 = 54°$.

steps.note: If they do not add to 360, find the slip before drawing.

steps.text: Draw a radius, measure the first angle from it with a protractor, and draw the next sector from the line you have just drawn. Label every sector.

visuals.alt: A table turning each frequency into an angle at 6 degrees per student: walk 126, bus 108, car 72, cycle 54, total 360 degrees
A pie chart of how 60 students travel to school, sectors of 126 degrees for walk, 108 for bus, 72 for car and 54 for cycle

visuals.problem: A pie chart shows how 90 people answered a survey question. The sector for Yes is 120°. How many people said Yes?

steps.text: The Yes sector is $\dfrac{120}{360} = \dfrac{1}{3}$ of the circle.
So it is a third of the 90 people: $\dfrac{1}{3} \times 90 = 30$ people.

visuals.alt: A pie chart of 90 people’s answers to a survey question: Yes 120 degrees, No 180 degrees and Unsure 60 degrees

check.prompt: In a survey of 60 students, 18 travel to school by bus. What angle does the Bus sector need in a pie chart?
check.solution: Each student gets $360 \div 60 = 6°$. The Bus sector is $18 \times 6 = 108°$.

steps.title: Two-way tables
steps.body:
A **two-way table** counts one group in two ways at once: here, boys and girls **and** how they travel. Each cell is the number of people who fit **both** its row and its column.

The rows and columns end in **totals**, and every row and every column must add up to its total. That is what lets a table with blanks be completed: find a row or a column with only one blank, and subtract.

props.title: Some cells given; find the rest

visuals.alt: A two-way table of boys and girls against way to school, with some cells blank: boys walk 12, boys bus 8, boys cycle 5, girls bus 10, girls car 7, girls total 30, total walk 21 and overall total 60

visuals.problem: Complete the two-way table of how 60 students travel to school.

steps.text: Boys total: the girls are 30 out of 60, so boys $= 60 - 30 = 30$.
Boys by car: the boys row has one blank left, so $30 - 12 - 8 - 5 = 5$.
steps.note: Look for a line with only one blank.

steps.text: Girls who walk: the Walk column totals 21, so $21 - 12 = 9$.
Girls who cycle: the girls row gives $30 - 9 - 10 - 7 = 4$.

steps.note: Both the bottom row and the right-hand column must reach the same grand total.

props.title: Every row and every column adds up

visuals.alt: The completed two-way table: boys 12, 8, 5, 5, total 30; girls 9, 10, 7, 4, total 30; totals 21, 18, 12, 9 and 60

check.prompt: A two-way table records 50 people and whether they own a dog. 28 of the people are adults, 12 of the adults own a dog, and 30 people own a dog altogether. How many of the children own a dog?
check.solution: The dog owners total is 30, and 12 of them are adults. So the children who own a dog are $30 - 12 = 18$.

steps.title: Time series: tables and line graphs
steps.body:
**Time series data** is one quantity measured at regular times. It is shown in a **table**, and as a **line graph** with **time along the horizontal axis**, the points plotted and joined with straight lines.

An ice cream shop recorded its sales each quarter (three months) for two years. The line graph shows two things at once:

- **A seasonal pattern.** Sales peak in **quarter 3**, July to September, and are lowest in quarter 1, every year. The shape repeats.
- **A trend.** Every quarter of year 2 is higher than the same quarter of year 1 (up 3, 4, 5, 3 hundred), so the overall direction is **upwards**.

**Compare like with like.** From quarter 3 to quarter 4 of year 2 sales fell by 28 hundred, but that is autumn arriving, not the business failing. To judge the trend, compare the same quarter in different years.

The lines between the points only show the direction of change. A point halfway along a line is not a sales figure: sales were counted per quarter, not in between.

visuals.alt: A table of ice creams sold each quarter, in hundreds: year 1 quarters 1 to 4 sold 12, 30, 44 and 18; year 2 sold 15, 34, 49 and 21

A time-series line graph of ice creams sold over eight quarters, the points joined by straight lines: a peak in quarter 3 of each year and a low in quarter 1, with every year-2 point higher than the same quarter of year 1

check.prompt: An ice cream shop sold these numbers each quarter, in hundreds. Year 1: 12, 30, 44, 18. Year 2: 15, 34, 49, 21. Which statement describes the data best?
check.solution: In both years the highest quarter is quarter 3, a **seasonal** pattern, and every quarter of year 2 beats the same quarter of year 1 (by 3, 4, 5, 3 hundred): **peaks each quarter 3; rising year on year**.

markScheme.description: seasonal peak in quarter 3 and a rising trend

options: Sales fall steadily from quarter 3 onwards
Peaks each quarter 3; rising year on year
Sales are the same every year, with no trend
Sales rise every single quarter without a fall

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**1.** In a survey of 30 people, 7 chose red. What angle is the red sector of a pie chart?

**2.** In a pictogram, one circle stands for 6 cars. A row has 2 whole circles and half a circle. How many cars is that?

**3.** In a two-way table of 40 people, 22 are adults. How many are children?

**4.** Which chart would you use for the number of goals scored in each of 20 matches?

**Answers.** 1. $360 \div 30 = 12°$ per person, so $7 \times 12 = 84°$. 2. $2 \times 6 + 3 = 15$ cars. 3. $40 - 22 = 18$. 4. A **vertical line chart**, because goals are discrete whole numbers.

visuals.alt: A table of answers to the four practice questions: 84 degrees, 15 cars, 18 children and a vertical line chart

check.prompt: A weather station records the temperature at noon every day for a year. Which is the best way to show it?
check.solution: This is **time series** data: one measurement at each point in time. **A line graph with time along the bottom** shows how it changes and any seasonal pattern. A pie chart shows parts of a whole, and temperatures are not parts of anything.

markScheme.description: a line graph with time on the horizontal axis

options: A dual bar chart of the hot and cold days
A pie chart with a sector for each day
A pictogram with a sun for each degree
A line graph with time along the bottom

steps.title: Going deeper: comparing pie charts, and charts that mislead
steps.body:
**A pie chart shows shares, not numbers.** School A has 120 students and School B has 480. Walk is 90° on A's pie and only 45° on B's. B's sector is half the size, yet it stands for $\dfrac{45}{360} \times 480 = 60$ students against A's $\dfrac{90}{360} \times 120 = 30$. Comparing sector sizes across two pies only compares **proportions**; to compare **how many**, turn each angle back into a frequency.

**Finding the total from one sector.** If a 40° sector stands for 18 people, then 360° is $\dfrac{360}{40} = 9$ times as many: $9 \times 18 = 162$ people.

**Criticising a chart.** When asked what is wrong with a chart, look for the faults in the table below. The first to check is the **vertical axis**. A bar chart's axis should start at 0. A line graph of values far from zero, such as daily temperatures, is often drawn on a zoomed axis, and that is fair when the break is shown and the change is not overstated. It misleads when the break is hidden or the picture makes a change look bigger than it is. Customer satisfaction that rose from 96% to 99% looks like a steep climb on an axis from 95% with no break marked, and like a flat line on an axis from 0%. Both graphs are drawn from the same five numbers.

A good criticism names the fault **and** its effect: *the vertical axis starts at 95 with no break shown, so a rise of 3 percentage points looks like the figure has quadrupled.*

visuals.alt: A line graph of customer satisfaction over five years with the vertical axis starting at 95 percent, so a rise from 96 to 99 percent climbs almost the full height of the graph
The same satisfaction figures on an axis from 0 to 100 percent: the line is almost flat near the top, rising from 96 to 99

A table of five ways a chart can mislead: an axis that is cut without the break being shown, an uneven scale, pictogram symbols of different sizes, no key or labels, and a three-dimensional pie chart, with the effect of each

check.prompt: School A has 120 students and School B has 480. On pie charts of how the students travel, Walk is 90° for School A and 45° for School B. Which school has more students who walk?
check.solution: Turn each angle back into people. School A: $\dfrac{90}{360} \times 120 = 30$. School B: $\dfrac{45}{360} \times 480 = 60$. So **School B, 60 walkers against 30**. A pie chart shows **shares**, and a smaller share of a much bigger school can be more people.

markScheme.description: School B, 60 against 30

options: Neither: the two pies show equal numbers
School A: its Walk sector is twice the angle
School B: 60 walkers against 30
It cannot be told from two pie charts

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Categorical** data (words): bar chart, pie chart or pictogram.
- **Discrete numerical** data (whole numbers): vertical line chart.
- **Time series** (over time): a table and a line graph, time along the bottom.
- A **frequency table** lists each category or value with how often it occurs; the frequencies add to the total.
- **Bar charts**: frequency up the side from 0, equal widths, gaps, labelled axes.
- **Dual bar charts** put two groups side by side to compare them; a **composite** bar stacks them.
- **Pictograms**: one symbol = the key; read whole symbols, then the part.
- **Pie charts**: angle = frequency ÷ total × 360°. Find the angle for one item first; the angles add to 360°.
- Reading back: frequency = angle ÷ 360° × total.
- **Two-way tables**: every row and column adds to its total; fill blanks by subtracting.
- **Time series**: look for the **trend** and the **seasonal pattern**, and compare like with like.
- A pie chart shows **shares**; two pies of different totals cannot be compared by sector size.
- *Zero or zoomed?* A bar chart starts at 0; a zoomed line graph needs its break shown and must not overstate the change.

questions.prompt: 60 students were asked how they travel to school. 21 of them walk. What angle is the Walk sector of a pie chart?
questions.solution: Each student gets $360 \div 60 = 6°$, so Walk is $21 \times 6 = 126°$. Using the frequency, 21, as the angle is the usual slip.

questions.prompt: In a pictogram, one square stands for 4 books. Wednesday’s row shows 4 whole symbols and a half of a symbol. How many books were borrowed on Wednesday?
questions.solution: Four whole squares are $4 \times 4 = 16$ books, and half a square is 2 more: $16 + 2 = 18$ books.

questions.prompt: A dual bar chart shows how boys and girls travel to school. The boys’ Walk bar reaches 12 and the girls’ Walk bar reaches 9. How many more boys than girls walk to school?
questions.solution: $12 - 9 = 3$ more boys walk.

visual.alt: A dual bar chart of how boys and girls travel to school, the two bars for each way side by side: walk 12 boys and 9 girls, bus 8 and 10, car 5 and 7, cycle 5 and 4

questions.prompt: A vertical line chart shows the number of people in each of 30 cars. 14 cars had 1 person, 9 had 2, 4 had 3 and 3 had 4. How many cars had 3 or more people in them?
questions.solution: 3 people or 4 people: $4 + 3 = 7$ cars.

visual.alt: A vertical line chart of the number of people in each of 30 cars: 1 person 14 cars, 2 people 9 cars, 3 people 4 cars and 4 people 3 cars, drawn as thin lines rather than bars

questions.prompt: In a survey of 40 people, 11 chose rugby as their favourite sport. What angle is the rugby sector of a pie chart?
questions.solution: Each person gets $360 \div 40 = 9°$, so rugby is $11 \times 9 = 99°$.

questions.prompt: A pie chart shows how 90 people answered a survey question. The sector for Yes has an angle of 120°. How many people answered Yes?
questions.solution: $\dfrac{120}{360} \times 90 = 30$ people. The sector is a third of the circle, so it is a third of the people.

visual.alt: A pie chart of 90 people’s answers to a survey question: Yes 120 degrees, No 180 degrees and Unsure 60 degrees

questions.prompt: In a pictogram of books borrowed, one square stands for 4 books. The rows show: Monday 2 whole symbols and a half of a symbol; Tuesday 3 whole symbols and a half of a symbol; Wednesday 4 whole symbols and a half of a symbol; Thursday 1 whole symbol and three quarters of a symbol; Friday 3 whole symbols and a quarter of a symbol. How many books were borrowed in the whole week?
questions.solution: Row by row: Mon 10, Tue 14, Wed 18, Thu 7, Fri 13. Total: $10 + 14 + 18 + 7 + 13 = 62$ books. (Or count all the symbols: $15.5 \times 4 = 62$.)

questions.solution: Compare like with like. Each quarter of year 2 beats the same quarter of year 1 (by 3, 4, 5, 3 hundred), so the trend is **upwards: each quarter beats the year before**. The fall after quarter 3 is seasonal, and it happens in both years.

questions.solution: Year 11: $80 - 45 = 35$ students. Not hockey: $35 - 14 = 21$.

questions.solution: A pie chart shows each category as a **share of the whole**, so it answers *what fraction of all the students walk?* at a glance. Exact counts are easier to read from a bar chart, and a change over time needs a time series.

markScheme.description: what fraction walk

questions.prompt: In a pie chart of favourite sports, the Tennis sector has an angle of 40° and represents 18 people. How many people were surveyed altogether?
questions.solution: 40° goes into 360° $\dfrac{360}{40} = 9$ times, so the whole survey is $9 \times 18 = 162$ people. Equivalently, each person is $\dfrac{40}{18}°$.

markScheme.description: 360 ÷ 40 = 9, or 40/18 degrees per person

questions.prompt: School A has 120 students and School B has 480. On pie charts of how the students travel, the Walk sector is 90° for School A and 45° for School B. A newspaper says “more students walk at School A”. Is it right?
questions.solution: Turn the angles into people: A has $\dfrac{90}{360} \times 120 = 30$, B has $\dfrac{45}{360} \times 480 = 60$. So **no: School B has 60 walkers, A has 30**. The sector sizes compare shares, not numbers.

questions.prompt: A company's graph shows customer satisfaction over five years as 96%, 97%, 97%, 98%, 99%. The vertical axis runs from 95% to 100%, with no break marked, and the company says satisfaction has soared. Why is the graph misleading?
questions.solution: **The cut axis makes a small rise look huge.** Nothing marks the break at 95, and the line climbs from 1 unit to 4 units above the bottom, as if satisfaction quadrupled, when it rose by 3 percentage points. A zoomed axis is not wrong in itself (a line graph of temperatures is usually drawn that way), so not every axis must start at 0; here the hidden break and the word *soared* overstate the change.

questions.solution: **A pie shows parts of a whole, not change.** This is time series data: twelve monthly temperatures do not add up to a meaningful whole, and the question is how the temperature **changes** through the year, which a line graph with the months along the bottom shows.

questions.prompt: 90 people went to a cinema. Two fifths of them were adults and the rest were children. Two thirds of the children bought popcorn. 40 people bought popcorn altogether. Using a two-way table, find how many adults did not buy popcorn.
questions.solution: Adults: $\dfrac{2}{5} \times 90 = 36$; children: $90 - 36 = 54$. Children with popcorn: $\dfrac{2}{3} \times 54 = 36$. Adults with popcorn: $40 - 36 = 4$. Adults without: $36 - 4 = 32$.

children with popcorn 36

questions.prompt: Three charities share a donation in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4. The shares are shown on a pie chart. What is the angle of the largest sector?

questions.solution: The same drop happened in year 1 (44 to 18), so it is **seasonal**, and both quarters are up on year 1 (44 to 49, 18 to 21). **No: it is the usual autumn fall, and both are up on year 1.**

questions.prompt: A café sold 45 drinks one morning: tea 18, coffee 15, juice 12. (a) Work out the angle of each sector of a pie chart of these drinks. (b) The café's second branch sold 90 drinks that morning, and its pie chart also has a juice sector of 96°. The owner says both branches sold the same number of juices. Is she right? Show your working.
questions.solution:
(a) Each drink gets $360 \div 45 = 8°$. Tea: $18 \times 8 = 144°$. Coffee: $15 \times 8 = 120°$. Juice: $12 \times 8 = 96°$. Check: $144 + 120 + 96 = 360°$.

(b) At the second branch the juice sector stands for $\dfrac{96}{360} \times 90 = 24$ juices, against 12 at the first. She is wrong. The two sectors have the same angle because juice is the same **share** of each branch's sales, but the second branch sold twice as many drinks, so it sold twice as many juices.

questions.prompt: A company's leaflet shows a line graph of customer satisfaction over five years: 96%, 97%, 97%, 98%, 99%. The vertical axis runs from 95% to 100%, with no break marked. Beside it is a pictogram in which the symbol for year 5 is drawn twice as tall and twice as wide as the symbol for year 1. The leaflet says satisfaction has “soared”. Evaluate the leaflet's presentation of the data.
questions.solution:
The line graph's vertical axis starts at 95%, and nothing marks the break. A zoomed axis can be fair on a line graph, but not when it hides the break and the picture overstates the change, as here. On that axis the first point is 1 unit above the bottom and the last is 4 units above it, so the line looks as if satisfaction has quadrupled. In fact it rose from 96% to 99%, which is 3 percentage points.

The pictogram is misleading in a different way. Every symbol in a pictogram should be the same size, with more symbols meaning more. A symbol twice as tall and twice as wide covers four times the area, so the eye reads a fourfold increase where there was a small one.

None of the numbers is false, but both pictures exaggerate. A fair summary is that satisfaction rose slightly, by 3 percentage points, from a level that was already high. "Soared" is not supported by the data.

examTechnique.body:
**Name the data before choosing the chart.** Words: bar chart, pie chart or pictogram. Whole numbers: vertical line chart. Measurements over time: a table and a line graph with time along the bottom.

**For a pie chart, write the angle for one item first**, then multiply each frequency by it, and add the angles to check they make 360° before drawing. Draw with a protractor from a radius, label every sector, and keep each angle to within a couple of degrees.

**To read a pie chart, divide the angle by 360 and multiply by the total.** If the total is not given, find it from a sector whose frequency you know.

**Read the key of a pictogram before counting symbols**, and work out what each part symbol is worth.

**Complete a two-way table from a row or column with one blank**, then check that every row and column adds to its total.

**When asked what is wrong with a chart**, name the fault and say what effect it has on the reader.
examinerErrors: Using each frequency as its pie chart angle instead of scaling to 360°.
Pie chart angles that do not add up to 360°, left unchecked.
Reading a pictogram part symbol as a whole symbol, or ignoring the key.
Bars of different widths, or no gaps, on a bar chart of categories.
A frequency axis with an uneven scale, or unlabelled axes.
Comparing sector sizes on two pie charts drawn from different totals.
Describing a seasonal fall as a downward trend without comparing the same season in each year.
Saying a chart is "wrong" without naming the fault or its effect.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer chooses the chart from the kind of data and says why: shares of a whole for a pie chart, separate whole numbers for a vertical line chart, change over time for a line graph. It builds a pie chart through the angle for one item and checks the angles make 360°, and reads one back through the same fraction, finding the total from a known sector when none is given. When two pie charts are compared, it turns angles back into frequencies before saying which group has more. On a time series it separates the seasonal pattern from the trend by comparing the same season in different years. Asked to criticise a chart, it names each fault, says what effect it has on a reader, and gives the fair conclusion the data supports.
